payload.stem: The potential energy of a particle on the $x$-axis is $U(x)=\left(\frac{x^3}{3}-\frac{7x^2}{2}+10x\right)$ (in joules, with $x$ in meters). Which statement about an equilibrium position of the particle is correct and best justified?

options.text: The stable equilibrium is at $x=2\text{ m}$, because the force is zero there and $d^2U/dx^2<0$, so $U$ has a local minimum.
options.why: Mislabels the maximum of $U$ at $x=2$ as a minimum; a negative second derivative means a maximum, which is unstable.

options.text: The stable equilibrium is at $x=0$, because $U=0$ there, so the particle has no potential energy to lose.
options.why: Confuses a zero of the potential energy with an equilibrium position, where the force would have to be zero.

options.text: The stable equilibrium is at $x=5\text{ m}$, because the force is zero there and $d^2U/dx^2>0$, so $U$ has a local minimum.
options.why: $dU/dx=1(x-2)(x-5)$ is zero at $x=2$ and $x=5$; $d^2U/dx^2$ is positive only at $x=5$, which is a minimum of $U$.

options.text: The stable equilibrium is at $x=3.5\text{ m}$, because $d^2U/dx^2=0$ there, so the curvature of $U$ vanishes.
options.why: Sets the second derivative to zero instead of the first, which locates the inflection point where the force is not zero.

options.why: The speeds follow $v^2=2gh(1-\mu/\tan\theta)$, which rank D > B > A > C.

payload.stem: A perpendicular force of $20\text{ N}$ is applied at one end of a light rod. The rod can rotate about a pivot at point A, which is $0.2\text{ m}$ from the end where the force is applied, or about a pivot at point B, which is $0.8\text{ m}$ from that end. Which statement comparing the torque of the force about A and about B is correct and best justified?

options.text: The torque about A is greater, $16.0\text{ N·m}$ compared with $4.00\text{ N·m}$ about B, because A is nearer to the force, so the force acts more directly.
options.why: Reverses the dependence on the lever arm, thinking that a pivot nearer the force gives a larger torque.

options.text: The torques about A and B are equal, $4.00\text{ N·m}$ in both cases, because the same $20\text{ N}$ force acts at the same point of the rod.
options.why: Believes the torque depends only on the force and not on the pivot position.

options.text: The torque about B is greater, $16.0\text{ N·m}$ compared with $4.00\text{ N·m}$ about A, because B is farther from the center of the rod.
options.why: Gets the right comparison for the wrong reason: the lever arm is measured from the pivot to the force, not from the center of the rod.

options.text: The torque about B is greater, $16.0\text{ N·m}$ compared with $4.00\text{ N·m}$ about A, because B is farther from where the force acts, so the lever arm is longer.
options.why: Torque is $rF\sin\theta$; with the same perpendicular force it grows in proportion to the distance from the pivot.

payload.stem: The graph shows the position of an oscillating block as a function of time. Which statement about the signs of the position, the velocity and the acceleration at $t=2.5\text{ s}$ is correct?

options.text: The position is negative, because the graph is below the axis; the velocity is positive, because the graph is rising; and the acceleration is negative.
options.why: Gives the acceleration the same sign as the position, instead of the opposite sign required by $a=-\omega^2x$.

options.text: The position is negative, because the graph is below the axis; the velocity is negative, because the graph is falling; and the acceleration is positive.
options.why: Reads the slope sign backward, taking a falling graph as a positive velocity or a rising graph as a negative one.

options.text: The position is positive, because the graph is above the axis; the velocity is positive, because the graph is rising; and the acceleration is negative.
options.why: Reads the sign of the position backward, taking a point above the axis as negative or a point below the axis as positive.

options.text: The position is negative, because the graph is below the axis; the velocity is positive, because the graph is rising; and the acceleration is positive.
options.why: The graph's height gives the sign of $x$, its slope gives the sign of $v$, and $a=-\omega^2x$ always has the sign opposite to $x$.

payload.title: Experiment: drag coefficient from terminal speeds

stimulus.description: A student drops small objects of different mass $m$ and the same shape through a tall column of viscous liquid and measures the constant (terminal) speed $v_t$ that each reaches. The liquid exerts a drag force of magnitude $bv$, where $b$ is an unknown constant.

notes: A student drops small objects of different mass $m$ and the same shape through a tall column of viscous liquid and measures the constant (terminal) speed $v_t$ that each reaches. The liquid exerts a drag force of magnitude $bv$, where $b$ is an unknown constant.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Describe an experimental procedure to collect the data for the terminal speed as a function of mass. Include the equipment and the measurements, how the independent variable is changed, and one way to reduce the uncertainty in the measured terminal speed.
parts.model_answer: Measure each mass with a balance; time the fall of each object between two marks that are far below the surface (after the speed is constant) with a stopwatch or video and divide the distance by the time; use objects of the same shape and the same liquid; reduce the uncertainty by using a longer timed distance or by repeating each drop and averaging.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies how the mass is measured and how the terminal speed is found (distance between marks divided by the time after the speed is constant)
required_elements: a way to measure the mass and a way to find the terminal speed
common_errors: times the fall from the surface including the speeding-up stage

rubric_rows.criterion: Changes only the mass while keeping the shape, the liquid and the temperature the same (both the shape and the liquid must be controlled)
required_elements: change only the mass and keep the shape and liquid

rubric_rows.criterion: Reduces the uncertainty by repeating each drop and averaging, or by using a longer timed distance (either earns the point)
required_elements: repeat and average or longer timed distance (either earns the point)

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Using Newton's second law at terminal speed, identify the quantities that should be plotted on the vertical and horizontal axes so that the data produce a straight line whose slope can be used to find $b$.
parts.model_answer: At terminal speed $mg=bv_t$, so $v_t=(g/b)m$: plot $v_t$ on the vertical axis against $m$ on the horizontal axis; the slope is $g/b$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies $v_t$ (vertical) versus $m$ (horizontal), or equivalently $mg$ versus $v_t$ with slope $b$ (either linear plot earns the point)
required_elements: v_t versus m or mg versus v_t (either earns the point)
alt_solutions: mg versus v_t, with slope b
common_errors: plots v_t versus m squared

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: On a blank grid whose scale you choose, plot the data and draw a best-fit line. Label the axes with quantities and units and use a scale that fills most of the grid.

rubric_rows.criterion: Axes are labeled with quantities and units and the scale fills most of the grid
